newsitem.title: USA: American pilots said "lack of trust" was obstacle.
newsitem.headline: American pilots said "lack of trust" was obstacle.

text.p: Pilots at American Airlines, which ratified a new five-year labour contract on Monday, said a "lack of trust" was the the biggest obstacle in the recent contract negotiations.
"The pilots have had a difficult time trusting the management of this corporation," said Jim Sovich, president of the Allied Pilots Association.
"We are absolutely committed to American Airlines and we felt, on many occassions, a comparable commitment from AMR Corp was lacking," Sovich said.
The union said 69.3 percent of its members voted to approve the new contract, with 5,661 pilots voting for ratification, compared to 2,507 pilots against, the union said.
Under the five-year contract, pilots will get a nine percent wage increase and 5.75 million stock options valued at $10 below Monday's average trading price of $93.375.
The deal includes a compromise on the most hotly contested issue regarding which pilots will fly new jets American plans to buy for its regional jet carrier, American Eagle.
The pilots and American Airlines had been in talks to finalise a new labour agreement since the current contract ran out on August 31, 1994.

The recent negotiations were marked by a brief pilot strike in February, intervention by President Bill Clinton and millions of dollars in lost revenues at American, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp.
With the new contract approved, the union offered a new challenge to the management of American Airlines.

"We expect you to live up to your end of the bargain by concentrating on and expanding the core airline. We expect you to use the relationship you develop with regional and foreign carriers to support American Airlines...not to supplant it," Sovich said.
American Airlines said it was pleased the pilots union ratified the contract.

"We are very pleased. It was a very nice, solid ratification. We wanted to have a very solid indication from the membership that they supported it, and we got that in almost every base," said American Airlines President Donald Carty.
